pumac-2009-power-02a.title: Smallest positive element
pumac-2009-power-02a.body: Let $L\subseteq\mathbb Z$ be a lattice. If $L=\{0\}$ then $L=0\cdot\mathbb Z$. Otherwise, by closure under negation $L$ contains a positive integer; let $d$ be the smallest. Every $d k$ lies in $L$ (closure under addition and negation), so $d\mathbb Z\subseteq L$. Conversely let $a\in L$ and write $a=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$. Then $r=a-qd\in L$, and minimality of $d$ forces $r=0$, so $d\mid a$ and $L\subseteq d\mathbb Z$. Hence $L=d\mathbb Z$. Conversely each $d\mathbb Z$ is clearly a lattice. ∎

pumac-2009-power-02b.title: Two directions
pumac-2009-power-02b.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Let $L$ be full and $\vec a\in\mathbb Z^n$. Choose $N>0$ with $N\vec a\in L$; then $N\vec a=\sum k_i\vec s_i$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z$, $\vec s_i\in S$, and $\vec a=\sum\frac{k_i}{N}\vec s_i$ is a rational combination.

($\Leftarrow$) Let $\vec a=\sum\frac{p_i}{q_i}\vec s_i$ with $p_i,q_i\in\mathbb Z$, $q_i>0$ (finitely many terms). Put $N=\prod q_i$. Then $N\vec a=\sum\left(p_i\prod_{j\ne i}q_j\right)\vec s_i$ is an integer combination of elements of $S$, so $N\vec a\in L$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-02c.title: The three vectors lie in a plane
pumac-2009-power-02c.body:
$(2,1,6)+(5,6,8)=(7,7,14)=7(1,1,2)$, so the third vector is a rational combination of the first two, and $L$ is just the lattice generated by $\vec a=(2,1,6)$ and $\vec b=(5,6,8)$ (with $\frac17(\vec a+\vec b)$ also in the span). All three vectors satisfy $-4x+2y+z=0$: $-8+2+6$, $-20+12+8$, $-4+2+2$ are all $0$. Hence every vector of $L$ lies in the plane $-4x+2y+z=0$. But $(0,0,N)$ is not in that plane for any $N\ne0$. So $L$ is not full.

**Answer: No**

pumac-2009-power-02c.title: Rational combinations
pumac-2009-power-02c.body:
By 2.2 we need every integer vector to be a rational combination. For $(0,0,1)=\alpha(2,1,6)+\beta(5,6,8)+\gamma(1,1,2)$ the first two coordinates give $2\alpha+5\beta+\gamma=0$, $\alpha+6\beta+\gamma=0$; subtracting gives $\alpha=\beta$, and then $\gamma=-7\alpha$ and the third coordinate is $6\alpha+8\alpha-14\alpha=0\neq1$. No solution, so the lattice is not full.

**Answer: No**

pumac-2009-power-02d.title: Invertible matrix
pumac-2009-power-02d.body:
The matrix with these vectors as rows has determinant $2(12-16)-1(10-8)+6(10-6)=-8-2+24=14\ne0$, so the three vectors are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ and span $\mathbb Q^3$. Every integer vector is then a rational combination of them (the inverse matrix has rational entries), so by 2.2 the lattice is full.

**Answer: Yes**

pumac-2009-power-02d.title: Explicit multiple
pumac-2009-power-02d.body:
By Cramer's rule $14\vec e_j$ is an integer combination of the three generators for each $j$ (the adjugate matrix has integer entries). So $14\vec a\in L$ for every $\vec a\in\mathbb Z^3$: $L$ is full.

**Answer: Yes**

pumac-2009-power-03a.title: Direct proof
pumac-2009-power-03a.body:
($\Rightarrow$) $\vec a=\vec a+\vec0\in\vec b+L$, so $\vec a=\vec b+\vec\ell$ for some $\vec\ell\in L$, and $\vec a-\vec b=\vec\ell\in L$.

($\Leftarrow$) Let $\vec a-\vec b\in L$. For $\vec\ell\in L$: $\vec a+\vec\ell=\vec b+\big((\vec a-\vec b)+\vec\ell\big)\in\vec b+L$, so $\vec a+L\subseteq\vec b+L$. Since $\vec b-\vec a=-(\vec a-\vec b)\in L$ too, the same argument with $\vec a,\vec b$ exchanged gives $\vec b+L\subseteq\vec a+L$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-03b.title: Contrapositive
pumac-2009-power-03b.body: Suppose $(\vec a+L)\cap(\vec b+L)\neq\varnothing$. Then $\vec a+\vec\ell_1=\vec b+\vec\ell_2$ for some $\vec\ell_1,\vec\ell_2\in L$, so $\vec a-\vec b=\vec\ell_2-\vec\ell_1\in L$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-03c.title: Characterise $L$
pumac-2009-power-03c.body:
**Claim:** $(a,b)\in L\iff3\mid a+b$. Elements of $L$ are $n(1,2)+m(2,1)=(n+2m,2n+m)$, with coordinate sum $3(n+m)$. Conversely if $3\mid a+b$, then put $n=b-\frac{a+b}3$ and $m=a-\frac{a+b}3$ (integers). Then $n(1,2)+m(2,1)$ has first coordinate $n+2m=b+2a-(a+b)=a$ and second coordinate $2n+m=2b+a-(a+b)=b$. So $(a,b)\in L$.

**Distinct:** the differences of $(0,0),(0,1),(0,2)$ are $(0,\pm1),(0,\pm2)$ with coordinate sums $\pm1,\pm2$, not divisible by $3$, so none lies in $L$ and the colattices are distinct by 3.1.

**No others:** given $(a,b)$, let $i\in\{0,1,2\}$ with $a+b\equiv i\pmod3$. Then $(a,b)-(0,i)$ has coordinate sum $a+b-i\equiv0$, so lies in $L$, and $(a,b)+L=(0,i)+L$ by 3.1.

Hence there are exactly $3$ colattices: $\det L=3$.

**Answer: 3**

pumac-2009-power-03d.title: Two directions
pumac-2009-power-03d.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Let $L\subseteq\mathbb Z^n$ be full. For each $i$ there is $N_i>0$ with $N_i\vec e_i\in L$. Given $\vec a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, write $a_i=q_iN_i+r_i$ with $0\le r_i<N_i$. Then $\vec a-(r_1,\dots,r_n)=\sum q_i(N_i\vec e_i)\in L$, so $\vec a+L=(r_1,\dots,r_n)+L$ by 3.1. Hence there are at most $N_1\cdots N_n$ colattices.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\det L<\infty$ and let $\vec a\in\mathbb Z^n$. The colattices $k\vec a+L$ ($k=1,2,3,\dots$) cannot all be distinct, so $k_1\vec a+L=k_2\vec a+L$ for some $k_1>k_2$. By 3.1, $(k_1-k_2)\vec a\in L$; take $N=k_1-k_2$. So $L$ is full. ∎

pumac-2009-power-03e.title: Counting in two steps
pumac-2009-power-03e.body:
Let $d=\operatorname{div}L$. Every vector of $L$ has all coordinates divisible by $d$, so $L\subseteq d\mathbb Z^n\subseteq\mathbb Z^n$. The lattice $d\mathbb Z^n$ has exactly $d^n$ colattices in $\mathbb Z^n$ (represented by $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ with $0\le a_i<d$). Because $L$ is full, $\det L<\infty$ (3.4).

Define $\varphi:\{\vec a+L\}\to\{\vec a+d\mathbb Z^n\}$ by $\vec a+L\mapsto\vec a+d\mathbb Z^n$; this is well defined (if $\vec a-\vec b\in L\subseteq d\mathbb Z^n$) and onto. The fibre over $\vec a+d\mathbb Z^n$ consists of the colattices $\vec a+\vec c+L$ with $\vec c\in d\mathbb Z^n$, and $\vec a+\vec c+L\mapsto\vec c+L$ is a bijection from this fibre to the fibre over $d\mathbb Z^n$ (the colattices of $L$ inside $d\mathbb Z^n$). So all fibres have the same size $k$ ($k$ is finite and positive), and
$$\det L=k\cdot d^n.$$
Thus $d^n\mid\det L$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-04a.title: A surjection that is not injective
pumac-2009-power-04a.body: If $\det L_2=\infty$ there is nothing to prove (either $\det L_1$ is finite, hence smaller, or both are infinite). So let $\det L_2<\infty$ and define $f:\vec a+L_2\mapsto\vec a+L_1$. It is well defined: if $\vec a-\vec b\in L_2\subseteq L_1$ then $\vec a+L_1=\vec b+L_1$. It is onto, since every colattice $\vec a+L_1$ is the image of $\vec a+L_2$. It is not injective: take $\vec\ell\in L_1\setminus L_2$; then $\vec\ell+L_2\ne L_2$ (3.1) but $f(\vec\ell+L_2)=\vec\ell+L_1=L_1=f(L_2)$. Hence $\det L_1<\det L_2$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-04b.title: Use the standard basis vectors
pumac-2009-power-04b.body: Let $L$ be full and choose positive integers $N_i$ with $N_i\vec e_i\in L$ ($i=1,\dots,n$). Let $K$ be the lattice generated by $\{N_1\vec e_1,\dots,N_n\vec e_n\}$: it is finitely generated and $K\subseteq L$ (integer combinations of elements of $L$ lie in $L$). $K$ is full: given $\vec a=\sum k_i\vec e_i\in\mathbb Z^n$, the vector $\left(\prod_jN_j\right)\vec a=\sum k_i\left(\prod_{j\ne i}N_j\right)(N_i\vec e_i)\in K$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-04c.title: Minimal determinant
pumac-2009-power-04c.body: Let $L$ be full. By 4.2 the set $\mathcal F$ of finitely generated full sublattices of $L$ is nonempty, and by 3.4 each member has a finite determinant. By well-ordering choose $M\in\mathcal F$ with the smallest determinant. Suppose $M\ne L$ and pick $\vec\ell\in L\setminus M$. The lattice $M'$ generated by the finitely many generators of $M$ together with $\vec\ell$ is finitely generated, contained in $L$, and full (it contains $M$). Also $M'\supsetneq M$, so $\det M'<\det M$ by 4.1, contradicting minimality. Hence $M=L$ and $L$ is finitely generated. ∎

pumac-2009-power-05a.title: Linear maps commute with integer scaling
pumac-2009-power-05a.body:
Let $f:\mathbb Z^n\to\mathbb Z^n$ be a linear bijection with $f(L_1)=L_2$. By induction $f(m\vec a)=mf(\vec a)$ for positive integers $m$ (since $f((m+1)\vec a)=f(m\vec a)+f(\vec a)$).

Let $d_i=\operatorname{div}L_i$. Every element of $L_1$ is $d_1\vec a$ with $\vec a\in\mathbb Z^n$, so every element of $L_2$ is $f(d_1\vec a)=d_1f(\vec a)$, which is divisible by $d_1$. Hence $d_1\mid$ all elements of $L_2$, so $d_1\le d_2$. Applying the same argument to the linear bijection $f^{-1}$, $d_2\le d_1$. So $d_1=d_2$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-05b.title: Bijection of colattices
pumac-2009-power-05b.body: Let $f$ be a linear bijection of $\mathbb Z^n$ with $f(L_1)=L_2$. Then $f(\vec a+L_1)=f(\vec a)+f(L_1)=f(\vec a)+L_2$, so $f$ sends colattices of $L_1$ to colattices of $L_2$; $f^{-1}$ (also linear) does the reverse, and the two maps are inverse to each other on colattices. Hence the colattices of $L_1$ and $L_2$ correspond bijectively: $\det L_1=\det L_2$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-05c.title: Explicit isomorphism
pumac-2009-power-05c.body:
Let $L_1=\langle(3,0),(0,5)\rangle=\{(3a,5b)\}$ and $L_2=\langle(1,0),(0,15)\rangle=\{(x,y):15\mid y\}$. Take $f(x,y)=(2x+y,\ 5x+3y)$, a linear bijection of $\mathbb Z^2$ (determinant $6-5=1$, inverse $(x,y)\mapsto(3x-y,-5x+2y)$). Then $f(3,0)=(6,15)\in L_2$ and $f(0,5)=(5,15)\in L_2$, so $f(L_1)\subseteq L_2$. Conversely $f(L_1)$ contains $(6,15)-(5,15)=(1,0)$ and $(5,15)-5(1,0)=(0,15)$, so $f(L_1)\supseteq\langle(1,0),(0,15)\rangle=L_2$. Hence $f(L_1)=L_2$, and $f$ is an isomorphism.

**Answer: Yes**

pumac-2009-power-05c.title: By invariants (5.6)
pumac-2009-power-05c.body:
Both lattices are full, have divisor $1$ (the generators $(3,0),(0,5)$ have $\gcd(3,5)=1$ as coordinates, and $(1,0)$ has coordinate gcd $1$) and determinant $15$ (index of $\{(3a,5b)\}$ is $3\cdot5$; index of $\{15\mid y\}$ is $15$). By 5.6 they are isomorphic.

**Answer: Yes**

pumac-2009-power-05d.title: Divisors differ
pumac-2009-power-05d.body:
The first lattice $\{(2a,4b)\}$ has divisor $2$ (all coordinates are even and $(2,0)$ is not divisible by $4$). The second contains $(1,0)$, so its divisor is $1$. The divisor is an isomorphism invariant (5.1), so they are not isomorphic. (Both have determinant $8$.)

**Answer: No**

pumac-2009-power-05e.title: Diagonal lattice
pumac-2009-power-05e.body: Let $L=\langle(d,0),(0,\Delta/d)\rangle$. Since $d^2\mid\Delta$, $d\mid\Delta/d$, so every vector of $L$ has both coordinates divisible by $d$; and $(d,0)\in L$ is not divisible by any larger integer, so $\operatorname{div}L=d$. The determinant: the vectors are $(dk,\frac\Delta dm)$, and the colattices are represented by $(r,s)$ with $0\le r<d$, $0\le s<\Delta/d$ (distinct by 3.1), so $\det L=d\cdot\frac\Delta d=\Delta$. ∎

pumac-2009-power-05f.title: Reduction to divisor 1
pumac-2009-power-05f.body:
Let $L$ be full in $\mathbb Z^2$ with $\operatorname{div}L=d$, $\det L=\Delta$. Then $L'=\{\vec a/d:\vec a\in L\}$ is a full lattice with divisor $1$ and $L=dL'$; scaling by $d$ preserves isomorphisms ($f(d\vec a)=df(\vec a)$), so it suffices to treat divisor $1$: we show such an $L$ is isomorphic to $\langle(1,0),(0,\Delta')\rangle$ where $\Delta'=\det L$. Since the determinant of $dL'$ is $d^2\det L'$, two lattices with the same $(d,\Delta)$ have $L',M'$ with the same determinant, so they are both isomorphic to the same standard lattice.

**Divisor 1.** Since $L$ is full, there is a smallest $E>0$ with $(E,0)\in L$, and the $y$-coordinates of vectors of $L$ form a lattice $C\mathbb Z$ with $C>0$. Choose $\vec b=(D,C)\in L$. Any $(x,y)\in L$ has $y=kC$, and $(x,y)-k\vec b=(x',0)\in L$ forces $E\mid x'$. Hence $L=\langle(E,0),(D,C)\rangle$. Its divisor is $\gcd(E,D,C)=1$.

*A primitive vector.* There is $k\in\mathbb Z$ with $\gcd(D+kE,C)=1$: for each prime $p\mid C$: if $p\mid E$ then $p\nmid D$ (as $\gcd(E,D,C)=1$), so $p\nmid D+kE$ for every $k$; if $p\nmid E$ choose $k\equiv0\pmod p$ when $p\nmid D$ and $k\equiv1$ when $p\mid D$; by the Chinese Remainder Theorem one $k$ works for all such $p$. So $\vec v=\vec b+k(E,0)=(p_0,C)\in L$ is primitive ($\gcd(p_0,C)=1$). Choose integers $x,y$ with $p_0x+Cy=1$ and put $N=\begin{pmatrix}p_0&-y\\C&x\end{pmatrix}$, $\det N=1$, $N(1,0)^T=\vec v$. The linear bijection $N^{-1}$ maps $\vec v$ to $(1,0)$, so $L$ is isomorphic to a lattice $L''\ni(1,0)$.

If $L''\ni(1,0)$, let $P>0$ be generator of its $y$-coordinates and $(c,P)\in L''$; then $(0,P)=(c,P)-c(1,0)\in L''$ and $L''=\langle(1,0),(0,P)\rangle$. Its determinant is $P$, and by 5.2 $P=\det L=\Delta$. So $L\cong\langle(1,0),(0,\Delta)\rangle$. ∎

**Conclusion.** For a full lattice with $\operatorname{div}L=d$, $\det L=\Delta$, we have $d^2\mid\Delta$ by 3.5, so the lattice of 5.5 with the same $(d,\Delta)$ exists, and by the above $L$ is isomorphic to it.

pumac-2009-power-05g.title: Two diagonal lattices
pumac-2009-power-05g.body:
$L_1=\{(x,y,z):2\mid y,\ 2\mid z\}$ and $L_2=\{(x,y,z):4\mid z\}$. Both contain $(1,0,0)$, so both have divisor $1$. Both have determinant $4$: colattices of $L_1$ are represented by $(0,y,z)$ with $y,z\in\{0,1\}$; those of $L_2$ by $(0,0,z)$ with $z\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ (distinct by 3.1).

They are not isomorphic. Property (*) of a lattice $L$: $2\vec a\in L$ for every $\vec a\in\mathbb Z^3$. Clearly $L_1$ has (*). Suppose $f:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb Z^3$ is a linear bijection with $f(L_1)=L_2$. For any $\vec b\in\mathbb Z^3$ write $\vec b=f(\vec a)$; then $2\vec b=f(2\vec a)\in f(L_1)=L_2$ because $2\vec a\in L_1$. So $L_2$ would have (*). But $2(0,0,1)=(0,0,2)\notin L_2$. Contradiction. ∎

pumac-2009-power-06a.title: Explicit change of basis
pumac-2009-power-06a.body:
Swap the first two coordinates (a linear bijection): the lattice becomes generated by $(2,2,0)$ and $(3,0,3)$. Then $(3,0,3)-(2,2,0)=(1,-2,3)=:\vec b_1$ and $(2,2,0)-2\vec b_1=(0,6,-6)=6\vec c$ with $\vec c=(0,1,-1)$; so the lattice is generated by $\vec b_1$ and $6\vec c$. The vectors $\vec b_1,\vec c,(0,0,1)$ form a basis of $\mathbb Z^3$ (determinant $1$), so after the linear bijection sending them to $\vec e_1,\vec e_2,\vec e_3$ the lattice is generated by $1\cdot\vec e_1$ and $6\vec e_2$, i.e. by $\{1\vec e_1,6\vec e_2,0\vec e_3\}$. The signature is $(1;6;0)$.

**Answer: (1;6;0)**

pumac-2009-power-06a.title: Minors
pumac-2009-power-06a.body:
Let $\Delta_k$ be the gcd of all $k\times k$ minors of the matrix whose rows are the generators. Row operations (changing generators) and column operations (linear bijections of $\mathbb Z^n$) do not change $\Delta_k$ and for a diagonal matrix $\Delta_k=d_1\cdots d_k$. Here the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&2&0\\0&3&3\end{pmatrix}$: $\Delta_1=\gcd(2,2,3,3)=1$, $\Delta_2=\gcd(6,6,6)=6$, $\Delta_3=0$. So $d_1=1$, $d_2=6$, $d_3=0$: signature $(1;6;0)$.

**Answer: (1;6;0)**

pumac-2009-power-06b.title: Gcd of minors
pumac-2009-power-06b.body:
Let $\Delta_k$ be the gcd of all $k\times k$ minors of the $4\times4$ matrix $M$ whose rows are the generators. Unimodular row operations (changing generators) and unimodular column operations (a linear bijection of $\mathbb Z^4$) do not change $\Delta_k$ (each new minor is an integer combination of old ones by Cauchy–Binet, and the operations are invertible), and for the diagonal matrix of Theorem 6.1, $\Delta_k=d_1\cdots d_k$. Computing: $\Delta_1=1$ (entries include $2$ and $5$), $\Delta_2=1$, $\Delta_3=3$, $\Delta_4=|\det M|=540$. Hence $d_1=1$, $d_2=\Delta_2/\Delta_1=1$, $d_3=\Delta_3/\Delta_2=3$, $d_4=\Delta_4/\Delta_3=180$.

**Answer: (1;1;3;180)**
